summary:
Indonesia is a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code, signed in December 2022 and effective 2 January 2026, penalises all consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, so the provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations; prosecution is reported as selective rather than systematic.

Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women, alongside national-level morality provisions. Aceh's punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and apply to anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors. In Aceh two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025.

Official hostility has escalated into state doctrine. In October 2025 President Prabowo Subianto issued a presidential decree listing the spread of LGBTQ culture as a non-military national threat, placing it alongside separatism and terrorism within national defense policy. Reporting in August 2026 (The Diplomat, 14 August 2026; ABC News, 15 August 2026) ties this decree to a documented surge in vigilante mob attacks on transgender women, with an academic commentator stating the regulation shifts rhetoric into the official doctrine of national defence policy, framing LGBTQ people as risks to be monitored and controlled.

Enforcement takes the form of venue-based raids. On 22 June 2025 police raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor and arrested 75 people (74 men, 1 woman) after public reports of a 'gay party'; Amnesty International stated the gathering violated no law and called the raid a blatant violation of human rights and privacy.

Expression is censored. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction criminalises any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to 7 years' imprisonment. In March 2016 the national broadcasting commission banned TV and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal. The government has banned websites and apps containing 'gay' or LGBTQ-related words including Grindr, and in 2025 a new bill was under discussion to explicitly prohibit online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour.

Death in custody is documented. In August 2022 Harvard student Rodrigo Ventocilla, a trans traveller on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges; his mother in Lima was told on a WhatsApp call that authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody, and his mother alleges police beat him. Indonesian police denied that violence was used in his death.

Human Rights Watch has documented discriminatory regulations, arrests and criminal trials against LGBT people in Indonesia since 2016. Its 7 July 2026 report records a surge in abuse against LGBT students following officials' condemnations of a student group at Universitas Indonesia, with the LGBT umbrella organization Arus Pelangi documenting 94 cases, and officials in early July 2026 calling on parents to monitor children in 'this lifestyle'.

As of 2019 no specific law protects Indonesian citizens from discrimination or harassment based on sexual orientation or gender identity. The police have issued a circular since 2015 to process hate speech related to sexual orientation and gender identity, and National Police Regulation Number 8 of 2009 stipulates a duty to protect minority groups' special rights including sexual orientation.
tangentialFactors:
The 2016 HRW report 'These Political Games Ruin Our Lives' records that the Indonesian Psychiatric Association proclaimed same-sex orientation and transgender identities mental illnesses and recommended psychological rehabilitation, while the Jokowi government remained mostly silent. This institutional framing predates the current escalation and informs how official bodies treat trans people today.

Indonesia's censorship regime reaches beyond broadcast into platform access: app bans, website blocks and account shutdowns (including the Instagram account of the comic Alpantuni in 2016) mean a visitor's own device-based social presence could fall foul of content rules if it presents LGBTQ material.

The October 2025 presidential decree places LGBTQ culture within national defense framing alongside separatism and terrorism, a categorisation that raises the stakes of any public visibility for visitors as well as residents. Reporting in August 2026 links this framing directly to vigilante attacks on transgender women.

Comparatively, Aceh operates a separate provincial religious-law layer on top of national statutes, so a visitor moving between provinces faces a different and more immediately physical penalty regime (public caning, as applied in February 2025) than in other parts of Indonesia.
localsOnly:
Transgender Indonesians can change their legal gender on official documents after undergoing sex reassignment surgery and receiving a judge's approval, after which they may marry someone of the opposite legal gender. Only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors are recognised, with no third gender or X option, and transgender Indonesians have their gender at birth printed on identification unless they have already obtained court recognition.

Since June 2021 the Ministry of Home Affairs has conducted outreach to issue transgender Indonesians with identification papers (Kartu Tanda Penduduk) across multiple provinces including Banten, West Java, Central Java, East Java, North Sumatra, South Sumatra, South Sulawesi, Lampung, and Papua, because many were undocumented, especially where families disapproved, leaving them without access to work or social services.

Since 2018 the Jakarta Social Agency has declared transgender women (waria) socially dysfunctional, regularly conducted raids against them, and taken detained trans individuals to city-owned rehabilitation centres where they are incarcerated alongside homeless people and released only after signing a promise not to repeat their offence; officials stated this is meant as a deterrent against being transgender.

Conversion therapy is widely practiced and openly advertised in rehabilitation centres, including corrective rape from family members against lesbian women. LGBTQ groups are working on setting up safe houses and evacuation plans. The Yayasan Srikandi Sejati organization provides HIV/AIDS counselling and free condoms to transgender sex workers at a free health clinic. Yogyakarta has the only madrasa for transgender people in the world.

Theoretically, protection against discriminatory employment practices on any ground is guaranteed in the Constitution and Human Rights Law (No. 39/1999). The Attorney General's Office rescinded a public job offer declaring LGBTQ persons need not apply after advice from the National Commission on Human Rights. A police brigadier (TT) was fired for being gay after colleagues outed him; his lawsuit was rejected by the Semarang State Administrative Court in May 2019 on procedural grounds.
outOfScopeNotes:
The claim that prosecution under the new penal code's extra-marital sex provision is selective rather than systematic rests on reporting summarised by Outright International (updated 12 March 2026); the underlying enforcement data and any per-prosecution breakdown are not sourced here and remain unresolved.

The 94 cases documented by Arus Pelangi, cited in the HRW report of 7 July 2026, are described as abuse against LGBT students broadly; the inventory does not break out how many involved transgender individuals specifically, so the trans-specific share is unresolved.

The August 2026 reporting on vigilante attacks on transgender women (The Diplomat 14 August 2026, ABC News 15 August 2026) describes a documented surge and ties it to the October 2025 presidential decree, but the inventory provides no incident count, fatality figure, or period total, so the magnitude of the surge is unresolved.

Rodrigo Ventocilla's death in custody (August 2022) is documented with a police denial of violence and a maternal allegation of beating; no adjudicated finding on cause of death appears in the inventory, so the outcome remains unresolved.

The 2025 bill to explicitly prohibit online content presenting LGBT behaviour is described as under discussion as of 2025; whether it has since been enacted is not sourced here and remains unresolved.
